GRU4Rec already learns input- and state-dependent update/reset gates; an additional item-conditioned forgetting gate therefore needs controls that isolate its incremental benefit. [GRU4Rec](https://arxiv.org/abs/1511.06939) establishes the backbone; [time-aware attentive memory research](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.08598) provides precedent for temporal gating in recurrent state transitions. Suggested ablations—not established findings for this task—are the corrected baseline, added gate fixed to one, learned constant scalar/vector decay, and item-conditioned decay, with identical training settings. Separately retrain each variant; deploy only one jointly trained GRU model per category. Compare gate values against training-item frequency and history position to check whether conditioning mainly reproduces popularity or recency.

Popularity-stratified evaluation is essential: [Prakash et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.17276) find that aggregate sequential-recommendation metrics conceal head/mid/tail differences, with random training negatives favoring head items and popularity-based sampling offering different accuracy–balance tradeoffs. For this experiment, retain the pinned candidates and report supplementary validation HR@10 by training-only target-frequency bands and history-length bins, including subgroup counts and paired hit changes. Cross-stratification can help separate longer-history gains from easier, popular targets; sparse cells limit conclusions.

[Krichene and Rendle](https://research.google/pubs/on-sampled-metrics-for-item-recommendation/) show sampled ranking metrics can reverse model comparisons relative to full-catalog metrics. Thus, HR@10 against 99 negatives supports claims about this fixed benchmark, not equivalent full-catalog accuracy. Keep the host evaluator unchanged and select by four-category macro validation HR@10; treat strata and gate statistics as diagnostics rather than replacement objectives.
